name: Shape Up
summary: Basecamp's product development method built on six-week cycles, work shaped at the right level of abstraction before it is bet on, and teams given full responsibility to deliver within a fixed time.
explanation:
Shape Up is a product development method described by Ryan Singer in the free book Shape Up: Stop Running in Circles and Ship Work that Matters (Basecamp, 2019). It replaces backlogs, sprints, and estimates with fixed time, shaped work, and deliberate bets.

## The Three Phases

- **Shaping**: Senior people define a problem, set an appetite (how much time it is worth), and sketch a solution at the right level of abstraction: concrete enough that the team knows what to build, rough enough to leave room for design decisions. Rabbit holes and no-gos are identified up front. The result is a pitch.
- **Betting**: At the betting table, stakeholders choose which pitches to bet the next cycle on. There is no backlog: pitches that are not chosen are not kept in a queue. Important ideas come back on their own.
- **Building**: A small team gets the whole cycle to deliver the shaped project. They define their own tasks, work on vertical slices, and track progress with hill charts. Scope is the variable: they cut and adjust to ship on time.

## Key Principles

- **Six-week cycles followed by a two-week cool-down** for fixing bugs, exploring, and planning.
- **Appetite instead of estimates**: Decide how much time a problem deserves, then design to fit it.
- **Fixed time, variable scope**: The deadline does not move. Scope is hammered to fit.
- **The circuit breaker**: If a project is not done by the end of the cycle, it does not get an automatic extension. It is stopped by default and must be re-shaped and re-bet.
- **Responsibility to the team**: Teams receive projects, not tasks, and are trusted to work out the details.

## Why It Matters

Shape Up addresses chronic problems of iterative methods: endless backlogs, projects that never end, and teams that never get uninterrupted time. It is also a good model for individuals: shape your projects before committing, give them a fixed budget, and accept that not everything you could do deserves to be done.
